question: What must a driver do before loading or unloading hazardous materials, per Section 9.4.1?
choice_a: Notify the National Response Center
choice_b: Turn on the hazard lights only
choice_c: Remove the vehicle's placards temporarily
choice_d: Set the parking brake and make sure the vehicle will not move
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states before loading or unloading, set the parking brake and make sure the vehicle will not move.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements

question: What tools are drivers told never to use when loading hazardous materials containers?
choice_a: Pallet jacks
choice_b: Hooks
choice_c: Forklifts
choice_d: Hand trucks
explanation: Section 9.4 states drivers must not use any tools that might damage containers during loading, and specifically must not use hooks.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4 Loading and Unloading

question: Why should hazardous materials be loaded away from heat sources, per Section 9.4.1?
choice_a: Because heat voids the shipper's insurance
choice_b: Because many products become more hazardous when exposed to heat
choice_c: Because heat interferes with placard adhesives
choice_d: Because it is only a fuel-efficiency concern
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states many products become more hazardous when exposed to heat, so hazardous materials should be loaded away from heat sources.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements

question: Is it legal to move a vehicle with leaking hazardous materials packages?
choice_a: Yes, if the driver notifies the shipper first
choice_b: Yes, as long as the destination is nearby
choice_c: Yes, if traveling under 25 mph
choice_d: No, it is illegal to move a vehicle with leaking hazardous materials
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states it is illegal to move a vehicle with leaking hazardous materials, warning 'LEAKS SPELL TROUBLE!'
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements

question: Around which hazard classes must smoking never occur when loading or unloading, per Section 9.4.1?
choice_a: Only Class 9 (Miscellaneous)
choice_b: Class 1 (Explosives), Class 2.1 (Flammable Gas), Class 3 (Flammable Liquids), Class 4 (Flammable Solids), and Class 5 (Oxidizers)
choice_c: Only Class 8 (Corrosives)
choice_d: Only Class 7 (Radioactive)
explanation: Section 9.4.1 lists Class 1, Class 2.1, Class 3, Class 4, and Class 5 as classes around which smoking is never allowed during loading or unloading.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, No Smoking

question: After loading, may a driver open a hazardous materials package during the trip?
choice_a: Only if the package is labeled Class 9
choice_b: Yes, to inspect the contents
choice_c: No, never open any package during the trip, and never transfer materials between packages while in transit
choice_d: Only with the shipper's verbal permission by phone
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states after loading, do not open any package during the trip and never transfer hazardous materials from one package to another while in transit (a cargo tank may be emptied, but not other packages).
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements

question: For which hazard classes do the cargo heater rules generally forbid the use of cargo heaters, including automatic heater/air conditioner units?
choice_a: Class 8 (Corrosives) only
choice_b: Class 9 (Miscellaneous) only
choice_c: Class 6 (Poison) and Class 7 (Radioactive)
choice_d: Class 1 (Explosives), Class 2.1 (Flammable Gas), and Class 3 (Flammable Liquids)
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states the cargo heater rules usually forbid using cargo heaters, including automatic heater/air conditioner units, for Class 1, Class 2.1, and Class 3 materials.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Cargo Heater Rules

question: Which hazard classes may NOT be carried as overhang or tailgate loads unless all packages are fire- and water-resistant or covered with a fire- and water-resistant tarp?
choice_a: Class 2 (Gases) only
choice_b: Class 1 (Explosives), Class 4 (Flammable Solids), and Class 5 (Oxidizers)
choice_c: Class 9 (Miscellaneous) only
choice_d: Class 6 (Poison) only
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states Class 1, Class 4, and Class 5 materials cannot be overhang or tailgate loads and must go in a closed cargo space unless all packages are fire and water resistant or covered with a resistant tarp.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Use Closed Cargo Space

question: Before loading or unloading explosives (Class 1), what must a driver do first?
choice_a: Apply extra placards to the trailer
choice_b: Contact CHEMTREC for authorization
choice_c: Increase the vehicle's idle speed
choice_d: Turn the engine off, then check the cargo space
explanation: The manual states to turn your engine off before loading or unloading any explosives, then check the cargo space.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 1 Explosives

question: What must be done to cargo heaters before loading Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives?
choice_a: Cover them with a fire-resistant tarp
choice_b: Set them to the lowest temperature setting
choice_c: Disable them: disconnect heater power sources and drain heater fuel tanks
choice_d: Nothing special is required for cargo heaters
explanation: The manual instructs to disable cargo heaters, disconnect heater power sources, and drain heater fuel tanks before loading explosives.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 1 Explosives

question: What type of floor lining material is required for Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives?
choice_a: Galvanized steel plate
choice_b: Stainless steel only
choice_c: No lining is required
choice_d: Non-metallic material or non-ferrous metal, with tight floors
explanation: The manual states the floors must be tight and the liner must be either non-metallic material or non-ferrous metal for Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 1 Explosives

question: When may Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives be transferred from one vehicle to another on a public roadway?
choice_a: Only in an emergency, with red warning reflectors, flags, or electric lanterns set out to warn others
choice_b: Only at night with headlights on
choice_c: Never, under any circumstance
choice_d: Anytime it is convenient for the driver
explanation: The manual states not to transfer Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives between vehicles on a public roadway except in an emergency, and if required, to set out red warning reflectors, flags, or electric lanterns.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 1 Explosives

question: May a driver transport a package of explosives that shows dampness or an oily stain?
choice_a: Yes, if placed at the rear of the trailer
choice_b: No, damaged packages of explosives showing dampness or an oily stain must never be transported
choice_c: Yes, if the shipper certifies it is safe
choice_d: Yes, as long as it is wrapped in plastic
explanation: The manual states never transport damaged packages of explosives, and specifically not to take a package that shows any dampness or oily stain.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 1 Explosives

question: What is true of Class 4 materials (Flammable Solids), per Section 9.4.1?
choice_a: They cannot cause fire under any condition
choice_b: They are solids that react, including with fire and explosion, to water, heat, and air, or that react spontaneously
choice_c: They are always liquids under pressure
choice_d: They are only regulated when transported by air
explanation: The manual describes Class 4 materials as solids that react, including fire and explosion, to water, heat, and air, or even react spontaneously.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 4 and 5 Materials

question: Class 4 and 5 materials that become unstable and dangerous when wet must be:
choice_a: Loaded only with corrosive liquids
choice_b: Sprayed lightly with water to reduce dust
choice_c: Stored only in open trailers
choice_d: Kept dry while in transit and during loading and unloading
explanation: The manual states Class 4 and 5 materials that become unstable and dangerous when wet must be kept dry while in transit and during loading and unloading.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 4 and 5 Materials

question: When hand-loading breakable containers of corrosive liquid, what should a driver do?
choice_a: Load them one by one, keep them right side up, and never drop or roll them
choice_b: Load them in bulk without individual handling
choice_c: Stack them on their sides to save space
choice_d: Load them last, on top of all other cargo
explanation: Section 9.4.1 states to load breakable containers of corrosive liquid one by one, keep them right side up, and not drop or roll the containers.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 8 Corrosives

question: What rule applies to loading nitric acid with other products, per Section 9.4.1?
choice_a: Nitric acid may only be transported with Division 1.1 explosives
choice_b: Nitric acid must always be loaded on top of other cargo
choice_c: Nitric acid has no special loading restrictions
choice_d: Do not load nitric acid above any other product
explanation: The manual states 'Do not load nitric acid above any other product.'
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 8 Corrosives

question: Charged storage batteries must be loaded so that:
choice_a: Their liquid won't spill, they are kept right side up, and other cargo won't fall against or short-circuit them
choice_b: They are placed loosely with no securing needed
choice_c: They are always loaded next to Division 1.1 explosives
choice_d: They are stacked upside down for stability
explanation: The manual states to load charged storage batteries so their liquid won't spill, keep them right side up, and make sure other cargo won't fall against or short circuit them.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 8 Corrosives

question: If a vehicle lacks racks to hold compressed gas cylinders, what must be true of the cargo space and cylinders, per Section 9.4.1?
choice_a: The floor must be flat, and cylinders must be held upright in racks or boxes that prevent turning over
choice_b: The cylinders may be loaded loose in any orientation
choice_c: Cylinders must be stacked three high without restraint
choice_d: The floor must be sloped toward the rear doors
explanation: The manual states that without racks, the cargo space floor must be flat, and cylinders must be held upright, in racks attached to the vehicle or in boxes that keep them from turning over.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 2 Compressed Gases

question: A package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD (Division 2.3 or 6.1) may never be loaded:
choice_a: Next to charged storage batteries
choice_b: On the same vehicle as any Class 9 material
choice_c: In the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food for human or animal consumption
choice_d: In a portable tank
explanation: The manual states never to load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD in the driver's cab or sleeper or with food material for human or animal consumption.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Division 2.3 and 6.1

question: What is the maximum total transport index allowed for all Class 7 (Radioactive) packages loaded on a single vehicle?
explanation: The manual states the total transport index of all packages in a single vehicle must not exceed 50.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 7 Radioactive

question: What does the 'transport index' printed on a Radioactive II or III labeled package tell a driver?
choice_a: The maximum speed allowed for the vehicle
choice_b: The package's exact weight in kilograms
choice_c: The number of placards required
choice_d: The degree of control needed during transportation, including closeness to people, animals, and unexposed film
explanation: The manual states the transport index tells the degree of control needed during transportation, controlling how close packages may be loaded to people, animals, and unexposed film.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Precautions for Specific Hazards, Class 7 Radioactive

question: Per the Do Not Load Table (Figure 9.9), Division 6.1 or 2.3 poison materials cannot be loaded in the same vehicle with:
choice_a: Tires and spare parts
choice_b: Empty fuel drums
choice_c: Animal or human food, unless the poison package is over-packed in an approved way
choice_d: Any Class 9 material
explanation: Figure 9.9 states Division 6.1 or 2.3 poison materials cannot be loaded with animal or human food unless the poison package is over-packed in an approved way; the manual notes foodstuffs are anything you swallow, but mouthwash, toothpaste, and skin creams are not foodstuffs.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Do Not Load Table, Figure 9.9

question: Per the manual's food definition used in the Do Not Load Table, which of these is NOT considered a 'foodstuff'?
choice_a: Bread
choice_b: Bottled juice
choice_c: Canned vegetables
choice_d: Mouthwash
explanation: The manual states foodstuffs are anything you swallow; however, mouthwash, toothpaste, and skin creams are explicitly not considered foodstuffs.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Do Not Load Table, Figure 9.9

question: According to Figure 9.9, charged storage batteries must not be loaded in the same vehicle with which explosives?
choice_a: Division 1.6 only
choice_b: Division 1.4 only
choice_c: Division 1.1
choice_d: Division 1.5 only
explanation: Figure 9.9's Do Not Load Table lists charged storage batteries as not to be loaded in the same vehicle with Division 1.1 explosives.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Do Not Load Table, Figure 9.9

question: Per Figure 9.9, materials that could release hydrocyanic acid (acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials) must not be loaded with:
choice_a: Division 6.1 cyanides or cyanide mixtures, such as sodium cyanide or silver cyanide
choice_b: Any flammable liquid
choice_c: Empty portable tanks
choice_d: Class 9 miscellaneous materials
explanation: Figure 9.9 states acids or other acidic materials that could release hydrocyanic acid must not be loaded with Division 6.1 cyanides or cyanide mixtures, giving examples such as cyanides, inorganic n.o.s., silver cyanide, and sodium cyanide.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Do Not Load Table, Figure 9.9

question: Where is a full list of materials that must be kept apart during loading found, beyond the examples in Figure 9.9?
choice_a: The vehicle's owner's manual
choice_b: The Emergency Response Guidebook only
choice_c: The Segregation Table for Hazardous Materials in the regulations
choice_d: There is no additional list; Figure 9.9 is exhaustive
explanation: The manual states the regulations (the Segregation Table for Hazardous Materials) name other materials that must be kept apart, beyond the examples shown in Figure 9.9.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.4.1 Mixed Loads

question: What is the difference between a cargo tank and a portable tank, per Section 9.5?
choice_a: Cargo tanks only carry gases while portable tanks only carry liquids
choice_b: Cargo tanks are permanently attached to the vehicle and remain on it during loading/unloading; portable tanks are not permanently attached and are loaded/unloaded off the vehicle
choice_c: Cargo tanks are always smaller than portable tanks
choice_d: There is no functional difference; the terms are interchangeable
explanation: Section 9.5 states cargo tanks are bulk packaging permanently attached to a vehicle and remain on the vehicle when loaded/unloaded, while portable tanks are not permanently attached and are loaded/unloaded off the vehicle before being put on for transportation.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5 Bulk Packaging Marking, Loading and Unloading

question: What are the two most common types of cargo tanks mentioned in Section 9.5, for liquids and gases respectively?
choice_a: Spec106A for liquids and Spec110A for gases
choice_b: MC307 for liquids and MC338 for gases
choice_c: DOT111 for liquids and DOT117 for gases
choice_d: MC306 for liquids and MC331 for gases
explanation: The manual states the most common cargo tanks are MC306 for liquids and MC331 for gases.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5 Bulk Packaging Marking, Loading and Unloading

question: What color and size are the identification numbers required on portable tanks, cargo tanks, and other bulk packaging?
choice_a: Blue 150 mm numbers on a green background
choice_b: Red 50 mm numbers on a yellow background
choice_c: Black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white diamond-shaped background
choice_d: White 25 mm numbers on a black background
explanation: Section 9.5.1 states the rules require black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white, diamond-shaped background if no placards are required.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: How tall must the shipping name letters be on a portable tank with a capacity of more than 1,000 gallons?
choice_a: At least one inch tall
choice_b: At least two inches tall
choice_c: At least four inches tall
choice_d: No minimum height is specified
explanation: Section 9.5.1 states the letters of the shipping name must be at least two inches tall on portable tanks with capacities of more than 1,000 gallons, and one inch tall on tanks under 1,000 gallons.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: Are Intermediate Bulk Containers (IBCs) required to display the owner's name or shipping name, per Section 9.5.1?
choice_a: Only the shipping name is required, never the owner's name
choice_b: Yes, both are always required
choice_c: No, IBCs are bulk packages but are not required to have the owner's name or shipping name
choice_d: Only if the IBC exceeds 1,000 gallons
explanation: Section 9.5.1 explicitly states Intermediate bulk containers (IBCs) are bulk packages but are not required to have the owner's name or shipping name.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: During loading or unloading of a cargo tank, the person watching must be within how many feet of the tank?
choice_a: 100 feet
choice_b: 25 feet
choice_c: 50 feet
choice_d: 10 feet
explanation: Section 9.5.2 requires the person watching the loading or unloading to be alert, have a clear view, and be within 25 feet of the tank.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.2 Tank Loading

question: What must be true before moving a cargo tank of hazardous materials, regardless of how small the amount or how short the distance?
choice_a: The placards must be removed
choice_b: The driver must radio the dispatcher
choice_c: All manholes and valves must be closed
choice_d: The tank must be completely empty
explanation: Section 9.5.2 states you must close all manholes and valves before moving a tank of hazardous materials, no matter how small the amount or how short the distance, and it is illegal to move a cargo tank with open valves or covers unless it is empty per 49 CFR 173.29.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.2 Tank Loading

question: What must a driver do to the cargo tank before opening the filling hole to load flammable liquids, per Section 9.5.3?
choice_a: Apply extra Class 3 placards
choice_b: Disconnect the tank from the trailer
choice_c: Ground the tank correctly and maintain the ground until after closing the filling hole
choice_d: Fill the tank to capacity before grounding
explanation: Section 9.5.3 states to ground a cargo tank correctly before opening the filling hole, and to maintain the ground until after closing the filling hole.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.3 Flammable Liquids

question: When should a driver's engine be running while loading or unloading flammable liquids?
choice_a: It should be left running at all times for safety
choice_b: Only when the tank is more than half full
choice_c: Only at night
choice_d: Only if needed to operate a pump; otherwise, turn off the engine
explanation: Section 9.5.3 states to turn off the engine before loading or unloading flammable liquids, only running it if needed to operate a pump.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.3 Flammable Liquids

question: Per Section 9.5.4, when should liquid discharge valves on a compressed gas tank be kept closed?
choice_a: At all times, even during loading
choice_b: Only when the vehicle is parked overnight
choice_c: Except when loading and unloading
choice_d: Only in cold weather
explanation: Section 9.5.4 states to keep liquid discharge valves on a compressed gas tank closed except when loading and unloading.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.4 Compressed Gas

question: Before coupling, uncoupling, or moving a cargo tank of compressed gas, what must a driver do?
choice_a: Unhook all loading/unloading connections and chock the trailer to prevent motion when uncoupled
choice_b: Remove the vehicle's placards
choice_c: Drain the tank completely
choice_d: Leave the hoses connected for a faster restart
explanation: Section 9.5.4 states to unhook all loading/unloading connections before coupling, uncoupling, or moving a cargo tank, and to always chock trailers and semi-trailers to prevent motion when uncoupled from the power unit.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.4 Compressed Gas

question: How close to the traveled part of the road may a vehicle carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives park?
choice_a: Never within five feet of the traveled part of the road
choice_b: There is no minimum distance
choice_c: No closer than 50 feet
choice_d: No closer than 100 feet
explanation: Section 9.6.1 states never to park with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: Except for short periods needed for vehicle operation (such as fueling), how close may a vehicle with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives park to a bridge, tunnel, building, or place where people gather?
choice_a: No closer than 100 feet
choice_b: No closer than 300 feet
choice_c: No closer than 1,000 feet
choice_d: No closer than 500 feet
explanation: Section 9.6.1 states not to park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, place where people gather, or an open fire, except briefly for vehicle operation necessities like fueling.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: What is a 'safe haven,' per Section 9.6.1?
choice_a: Any private residential driveway
choice_b: An approved place, usually designated by local authorities, for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives
choice_c: A rest area with a working payphone
choice_d: A truck stop with security cameras
explanation: The manual defines a safe haven as an approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, with designation usually made by local authorities.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: May a driver uncouple a trailer carrying hazardous materials and leave it on a public street?
choice_a: Yes, for up to one hour
choice_b: Yes, if a warning triangle is placed nearby
choice_c: No, per Section 9.6.2, do not uncouple a trailer and leave it with hazardous materials on a public street
choice_d: Yes, if the trailer is placarded correctly
explanation: Section 9.6.2 states do not uncouple a trailer and leave it with hazardous materials on a public street.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.2 Parking a Placarded Vehicle

question: Per Section 9.6.3, a person attending a placarded parked vehicle must be within how many feet of the vehicle if not inside it?
choice_a: 200 feet
choice_b: 100 feet, and have the vehicle within clear view
choice_c: 25 feet, with no view requirement
choice_d: 50 feet, with the vehicle out of view allowed
explanation: Section 9.6.3 states the attendant must be in the vehicle, awake, and not in the sleeper berth, or within 100 feet of the vehicle with it in clear view.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.3 Attending Parked Vehicles

question: Around which vehicles/loads must a driver never use burning signals such as flares or fuses, per Section 9.6.4?
choice_a: Only vehicles carrying Class 9 materials
choice_b: Any vehicle over 26,000 pounds GVWR
choice_c: Only vehicles without a fire extinguisher
choice_d: A tank used for Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) or Division 2.1 (Flammable Gas), loaded or empty, and any vehicle loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives
explanation: Section 9.6.4 states never to use burning signals such as flares or fuses around a tank used for Class 3 or Division 2.1 materials (loaded or empty) or a vehicle loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives; use reflective triangles or red electric lights instead.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.4 No Flares!

question: Whenever placarded, what should a driver avoid, per Section 9.6.5?
choice_a: Only rural back roads
choice_b: Only interstate highways
choice_c: Toll roads exclusively
choice_d: Heavily populated areas, crowds, tunnels, narrow streets, and alleys
explanation: Section 9.6.5 states whenever placarded, avoid heavily populated areas, crowds, tunnels, narrow streets, and alleys, taking other routes even if inconvenient.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.5 Route Restrictions

question: If transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what must the driver have and follow?
choice_a: A written route plan
choice_b: No special route documentation is required
choice_c: A verbal agreement with the shipper only
choice_d: A GPS tracking subscription
explanation: Section 9.6.5 states that if transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, the driver must have a written route plan and follow it, keeping a copy while transporting the explosives.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.5 Route Restrictions

question: For placarded radioactive materials, who is responsible for choosing the safest route?
choice_a: The state police
choice_b: The National Response Center
choice_c: The carrier, who must then tell the driver about the materials and show the route plan
choice_d: The driver alone, without carrier input
explanation: Section 9.6.5 states a carrier must choose the safest route to transport placarded radioactive materials and, after choosing the route, tell the driver about the radioactive materials and show the route plan.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.5 Route Restrictions

question: How close may a driver smoke to a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) or Division 2.1 (Gases)?
choice_a: Smoking is not allowed within 25 feet of such a tank
choice_b: 50 feet is the minimum distance
choice_c: There is no minimum distance restriction
choice_d: 10 feet is the minimum distance
explanation: Section 9.6.6 states not to smoke within 25 feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases).
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.6 No Smoking

question: Per Section 9.6.6, smoking or carrying a lighted cigarette, cigar, or pipe within 25 feet of a vehicle is prohibited if it contains:
choice_a: Only Class 9 (Miscellaneous) materials
choice_b: Class 1 (Explosives), Class 3 (Flammable Liquids), Class 4 (Flammable Solids), or Class 4.2 (Spontaneously Combustible)
choice_c: Only Class 8 (Corrosives)
choice_d: Only Class 7 (Radioactive) materials
explanation: Section 9.6.6 lists Class 1, Class 3, Class 4, and Class 4.2 as classes for which smoking or a lighted cigarette, cigar, or pipe is prohibited within 25 feet of the vehicle.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.6 No Smoking

question: What must a driver do before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials, per Section 9.6.7?
choice_a: Disconnect the trailer from the tractor
choice_b: Leave the engine running to keep the electrical system active
choice_c: Turn off the engine, and have someone always at the nozzle controlling fuel flow
choice_d: Remove all placards from the vehicle
explanation: Section 9.6.7 states to turn off the engine before fueling a vehicle containing hazardous materials, and someone must always be at the nozzle controlling fuel flow.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.7 Refuel with Engine Off

question: What UL rating fire extinguisher must the power unit of a placarded vehicle carry, per Section 9.6.8?
choice_a: No specific rating is required
choice_b: 5 B:C or more
choice_c: 20 A:B:C or more
choice_d: 10 B:C or more
explanation: Section 9.6.8 states the power unit of placarded vehicles must have a fire extinguisher with a UL rating of 10 B:C or more.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.8 10 B:C Fire Extinguisher

question: What is the only acceptable way to check tire pressure on a placarded vehicle, per Section 9.6.9?
choice_a: Visual inspection only
choice_b: Using a tire pressure gauge
choice_c: Kicking the tire
choice_d: Listening for hissing sounds
explanation: Section 9.6.9 states the only acceptable way to check tire pressure is to use a tire pressure gauge.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.9 Check Tires

question: When must a driver check the tires of a placarded vehicle with dual tires, per Section 9.6.9?
choice_a: Only before crossing state lines
choice_b: At the start of each trip and each time the vehicle stops
choice_c: Only if the tire pressure warning light illuminates
choice_d: Only once per week
explanation: Section 9.6.9 states to check placarded vehicles with dual tires at the start of each trip and when parked, checking the tires each time you stop.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.9 Check Tires

question: For a driver hauling Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what must the carrier provide besides the shipping papers?
choice_a: A copy of FMCSR Part 397 and written emergency instructions
choice_b: A company credit card
choice_c: A satellite phone
choice_d: Nothing beyond the standard shipping paper
explanation: Section 9.6.10 states a carrier must give each driver transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives a copy of FMCSR Part 397 and written instructions on what to do if delayed or in an accident.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.10 Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

question: A driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must have which special equipment in the vehicle, per Section 9.6.11?
choice_a: An approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings
choice_b: A second fire extinguisher only
choice_c: A hazmat suit and portable shower
choice_d: A backup cargo tank
explanation: Section 9.6.11 states a driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must have an approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings on the cargo tank.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.11 Equipment for Chlorine

question: How far before a railroad crossing must a placarded vehicle or one with cargo tanks (loaded or empty) stop, per Section 9.6.12?
choice_a: 100 to 150 feet before the nearest rail
choice_b: 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail
choice_c: Right at the crossing sign, regardless of distance
choice_d: 5 to 10 feet before the nearest rail
explanation: Section 9.6.12 states you must stop 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail, proceeding only when sure no train is coming and you can clear the tracks without stopping.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.12 Stop Before Railroad Crossings

question: Should a driver shift gears while crossing railroad tracks with a hazmat load, per Section 9.6.12?
choice_a: Yes, but only into a higher gear
choice_b: No, don't shift gears while crossing the tracks
choice_c: It depends on the number of tracks
choice_d: Yes, always downshift for extra power
explanation: Section 9.6.12 explicitly instructs 'Don't shift gears while crossing the tracks.'
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.12 Stop Before Railroad Crossings

question: What is the purpose of the DOT's Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG), per Section 9.7.1?
choice_a: To calculate freight charges for hazmat shipments
choice_b: To track driver hours of service
choice_c: To register new hazmat carriers with the DOT
choice_d: To help firefighters, police, and industry workers protect themselves and the public from hazardous materials
explanation: Section 9.7.1 states the ERG is a guidebook for firefighters, police, and industry workers on how to protect themselves and the public from hazardous materials, indexed by shipping name and identification number.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.1 Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)

question: According to the checklist in Section 9.7.2, what should a driver do at the scene of a hazmat crash or incident?
choice_a: Wait inside the cab until police arrive
choice_b: Move all cargo to a nearby vehicle
choice_c: Immediately attempt to repair the leaking package
choice_d: Check on the driving partner, keep shipping papers with you, keep people far away and upwind, and call for help
explanation: Section 9.7.2's checklist includes checking that your driving partner is OK, keeping shipping papers with you, keeping people far away and upwind, warning others, calling for help, and following employer's instructions.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.2 Crashes/Incidents

question: Before opening trailer doors during a suspected cargo fire, what should a driver do, per Section 9.7.3?
choice_a: Drive faster to create airflow
choice_b: Feel the doors to see if they are hot; if hot, do not open them
choice_c: Open the doors immediately to let smoke escape
choice_d: Spray water directly on the doors
explanation: Section 9.7.3 instructs drivers to feel trailer doors to see if they are hot before opening; if hot, there may be a cargo fire and the doors should not be opened, since air can make the fire flare up.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires

question: Should an untrained driver attempt to fight a hazardous materials cargo fire, per Section 9.7.3?
choice_a: Only if the fire is very small
choice_b: No, unless trained and equipped to do so safely, don't fight hazardous materials fires
choice_c: Only if a fire extinguisher rated 5 B:C is available
choice_d: Yes, all drivers are expected to fight cargo fires
explanation: Section 9.7.3 states that unless you have the training and equipment to do so safely, you should not fight hazardous materials fires, which require special training and protective gear.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires

question: Should a driver try to identify a leaking hazardous material by its smell, per Section 9.7.3?
choice_a: No, toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and can injure or kill you even if they don't smell
choice_b: Only for Class 3 flammable liquids
choice_c: Yes, smell is a reliable way to identify most hazardous materials
choice_d: Only if wearing a respirator
explanation: Section 9.7.3 warns not to try to identify the material or find the source of a leak by smell, since toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and can injure or kill you even if they don't smell.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires (Leak Response)

question: If hazardous materials are spilling from a vehicle, what four steps does Section 9.7.3 instruct the driver to take?
choice_a: Drive to the nearest truck stop, park, call the shipper, and wait
choice_b: Continue to the destination as quickly as possible
choice_c: Park it, secure the area, stay there, and send someone else for help
choice_d: Transfer the load to another vehicle immediately
explanation: Section 9.7.3 instructs: if hazardous materials are spilling from your vehicle, park it, secure the area, stay there, and send someone else for help.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires (Spill Response)

question: Why does Section 9.7.3 warn against continuing to drive with hazardous materials leaking from the vehicle to find a phone or truck stop?
choice_a: Because it voids the shipper's certification
choice_b: Because it violates hours-of-service rules
choice_c: Because it is only a fuel-economy concern
choice_d: Because the carrier pays for cleanup of contaminated areas, and the driver should not leave a lengthy trail of contamination
explanation: Section 9.7.3 explains the carrier pays for the cleanup of contaminated parking lots, roadways, and drainage ditches, so a driver should not leave a lengthy trail of contamination by continuing to drive.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires (Spill Response)

question: When sending someone else for help after a hazmat spill, what information should the driver give them, per Section 9.7.3?
choice_a: Nothing; simply wait for them to figure it out
choice_b: A description of the emergency, exact location and direction of travel, the driver's and carrier's names, and the shipping name/hazard class/ID number if known
choice_c: Only the driver's cell phone number
choice_d: Only the make and model of the truck
explanation: Section 9.7.3 lists a description of the emergency, exact location and direction of travel, the driver's name, the carrier's name, the terminal's community/city, and the proper shipping name, hazard class, and identification number if known.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires (Spill Response)

question: If a vehicle carrying explosives is involved in a collision, how far from the vehicles and occupied buildings should the explosives be placed before separating the vehicles?
choice_a: There is no specified distance
choice_b: At least 50 feet
choice_c: At least 200 feet
choice_d: At least 500 feet
explanation: Section 9.7.4 states to remove all explosives before separating vehicles involved in a collision, placing them at least 200 feet from the vehicles and occupied buildings, and to stay a safe distance away.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards, Class 1 Explosives

question: If compressed gas is leaking from a vehicle, per Section 9.7.4, whom must the driver notify?
choice_a: The shipper
choice_b: Only the local fire department
choice_c: No notification is required if the leak stops on its own
choice_d: Only the vehicle's manufacturer
explanation: Section 9.7.4 states you must notify the shipper if compressed gas is involved in any accident.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards, Class 2 Gases

question: If a Division 6.2 (Infectious Substances) package is damaged during handling or transportation, what should a driver do immediately?
choice_a: Dispose of the package at the nearest waste facility
choice_b: Repackage the material personally
choice_c: Contact the supervisor immediately
choice_d: Continue the delivery without reporting it
explanation: Section 9.7.4 states if a Division 6.2 (Infectious Substances) package is damaged in handling or transportation, you should immediately contact your supervisor, and damaged or leaking packages should not be accepted.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards, Class 6 Infectious Substances

question: If radioactive material is involved in a leak or broken package, when may the vehicle be used again, per Section 9.7.4?
choice_a: After 24 hours have passed
choice_b: Once the driver washes their hands
choice_c: Immediately, once the spill is wiped up
choice_d: Only after it is cleaned and checked with a survey meter
explanation: Section 9.7.4 states do not use the vehicle until it is cleaned and checked with a survey meter after a radioactive material leak or damaged package.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards, Class 7 Radioactive

question: After unloading a corrosive material and washing the vehicle's interior, when should this cleaning occur, per Section 9.7.4?
choice_a: Only if visible residue remains after 48 hours
choice_b: As soon as possible before reloading
choice_c: Only at the end of the work week
choice_d: Cleaning is optional for corrosives
explanation: Section 9.7.4 states parts of the vehicle exposed to a corrosive liquid must be thoroughly washed with water, and after unloading, the interior should be washed out as soon as possible before reloading.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards, Class 8 Corrosives

question: Which agency's 24-hour toll-free line helps coordinate emergency response to chemical hazards and must be called after certain hazmat incidents, per Section 9.7.5?
choice_a: The state Department of Labor
choice_b: The National Response Center
choice_c: The vehicle manufacturer's hotline
choice_d: The local Chamber of Commerce
explanation: Section 9.7.5 identifies the National Response Center as the agency that helps coordinate emergency response to chemical hazards, maintaining a 24-hour toll-free line.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: Per Section 9.7.5, which of these events requires notifying the National Response Center?
choice_a: The vehicle receives a routine inspection
choice_b: The driver takes a different route than planned
choice_c: The shipment arrives more than one hour late
choice_d: A person is killed, or estimated property damage exceeds $50,000
explanation: Section 9.7.5 lists reportable events including a death, hospitalization of an injured person, property damage exceeding $50,000, evacuation of the public for more than one hour, closure of a major transportation artery for an hour or more, and suspected radioactive contamination.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: What organization, besides the National Response Center, provides emergency personnel with technical information about the physical properties of hazardous materials via a 24-hour toll-free line?
choice_a: CHEMTREC (Chemical Transportation Emergency Center)
choice_b: The Environmental Protection Agency's regional office
choice_c: The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration
choice_d: The state Bureau of Motor Vehicles
explanation: Section 9.7.5 describes CHEMTREC in Washington as providing emergency personnel with technical information about the physical properties of hazardous materials, in close communication with the National Response Center.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification, CHEMTREC

question: Within how many days must a carrier make a detailed written report of a hazardous materials incident, per Section 9.7.5?
choice_a: 7 days
choice_b: 24 hours
choice_c: 90 days
choice_d: 30 days
explanation: Section 9.7.5 states carriers must make detailed written reports within 30 days of a hazardous materials incident.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: Per Table B (Figure 9.11) in Section 9.7, which materials are given as examples of the 'Miscellaneous Hazardous Materials' class?
choice_a: Formaldehyde and asbestos
choice_b: Uranium and plutonium
choice_c: Gasoline and acetone
choice_d: Hydrochloric acid and battery acid
explanation: Figure 9.11's Table B lists formaldehyde and asbestos as examples of Class 9, Miscellaneous Hazardous Materials.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7 Hazard Class Definitions, Table B, Figure 9.11

question: Per Table B (Figure 9.11), hair spray and charcoal are given as examples of which category?
choice_a: ORM-D (Other Regulated Material-Domestic)
choice_b: Combustible Liquids
choice_c: Corrosives
choice_d: Radioactive materials
explanation: Figure 9.11's Table B lists hair spray and charcoal as examples of ORM-D (Other Regulated Material-Domestic).
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7 Hazard Class Definitions, Table B, Figure 9.11

question: Per the Radioactive Separation Table (Figure 9.10) referenced in Section 9.7, what governs how long and how close a Yellow-II or Yellow-III labeled radioactive package may be left near people, animals, or film?
choice_a: The distance already traveled that day
choice_b: The package's weight only
choice_c: The package's transport index and the total exposure time shown in the table
choice_d: The time of day the delivery occurs
explanation: The manual states not to leave radioactive Yellow-II or Yellow-III labeled packages near people, animals, or film longer than shown in the Radioactive Separation Table (Figure 9.10), which is based on transport index and exposure time.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7 Radioactive Separation Table, Figure 9.10
